alternatives.label: People, environments and global change
alternatives.concept: A programme on people, environments and global change combining social theory, global economics and politics with environmental change, geospatial analysis, spatial engineering and sustainability governance. Applied delta research connects evidence to local questions; the programme does not reproduce a full human-geography or urban-planning curriculum.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines global social and political-economic study with environmental science, GIS, spatial engineering and governance. Spatial Planning adds applied geospatial projects, without a sustained urban-design, transport or land-development sequence.
progression: All current formal prerequisites and offerings are satisfied. Sustainability Essentials I precedes II, Earth Observation and Spatial Planning; Research Methods & Statistics precedes Public Economics, International Macroeconomics and Econometrics. Research in a Sustainable Delta is offered only in the first scheduled term and has no formal prerequisite. It is an early team inquiry, not an advanced individual thesis. Qualitative methods may precede introductory sociology under the open curriculum. Dynamic Earth follows earlier sustainability and climate foundations.

alternatives.label: Environmental transitions and delta resilience
alternatives.concept: A distinct environmental-science and sustainability pathway through Earth systems, climate, ecology, coastal hazards, water governance, renewable energy, circularity and applied delta research, with social research and civil-society study. It does not reproduce the Radboud dedicated spatial-planning and urbanisation curriculum.
alternatives.labelReason: The selected Earth science, climate, ecology, environmental governance, water and renewable systems courses sustain a different scientific focus from the first programme.
progression: All current formal prerequisites and offerings are satisfied. Sustainability Essentials I precedes II and Earth Observation; II precedes recycling, resources and renewable-system design. The only scheduled offering of Research in a Sustainable Delta is the first term and it has no formal prerequisite; it is an early team project, not advanced independent research. Dynamic Earth is placed at its available fifth term after hazards, climate and environmental foundations; its lack of a formal prerequisite permits this sequence.
alternatives.distinctness: The alternatives share 13 courses and differ by 11 courses (82.5 EC) each. The first develops global social theory, economics, political institutions and spatial engineering; the second instead develops biodiversity, conservation, hazards, life-cycle assessment, biogeochemistry, resources and renewable energy. These specialist priorities determine the differences.

candidates.label: Urbanisation and spatial planning
candidates.reason: Current Spatial Planning is offered in 2028h1 after Sustainability Essentials II, and Public Policy Analysis is offered in 2028h1/2029h1. Spatial Planning is incorporated into the closest programme. Its description supports spatial engineering and geospatial projects in disaster response, agriculture and environmental monitoring, not a dedicated urban-design, transport-geography or land-development sequence. A further governance/spatial-engineering variant would largely repeat the completed closest programme; replacing its global theory/economics with ecology, hazards and environmental technology instead approaches the included second programme. The available urban-relevant policy, nature-based infrastructure, law, sociology and economics provide useful contributions, but do not establish the sustained distinct city/land-development curriculum of the proposed urbanisation concept. The rejection follows actual course content and the completed alternatives, not unavailable offerings or absence of the degree title.

candidates.label: Secondary-school geography teaching
candidates.reason: Current official evidence supports an optional 30-EC Educative Minor with actual classroom practice. The current UCR catalogue offers related Earth/environmental study but no evidenced sequence in geography pedagogy, school-based teaching practice and supervised lesson development sufficient to organise a separate 24-course geography-education programme. The academic and practical shortfall, rather than absence of a licence alone, prevents this additional concept.

routeSelection.route: Globalisation thematic track (18 EC in year two; 6 EC thematic course in year three)

selection.assessment: Two content-grounded, distinct and feasible curricula respond to global social-environmental change and environmental transitions. The first now includes available spatial engineering. A separately assessed urbanisation concept lacks a distinct sustained city/land-development spine; a teaching concept lacks geography pedagogy and supervised school practice. Stop at two.

blocks: Both develop academic writing, source evaluation, research questions and responsible inquiry; UCR combines these skills with personal and community development rather than a dedicated GPM skills course.
Selected social sciences, environmental study and spatial engineering do not supply the integrated introductory disciplinary survey of geography, planning and environment.
Spatial engineering and nature-based interventions do not establish this component’s primary historical and social explanation of spatial transformations.

General social theory does not establish this dedicated theoretical treatment of space and environment.
Both develop qualitative research design, evidence collection and interpretation for social inquiry; UCR is not specifically a geographic fieldwork course.
Both develop introductory statistical analysis for empirical research. UCR also includes research design and a team project, without the GPM-specific applications.
Both use statistical modelling and empirical analysis; UCR specialises in econometric estimators, tests and an empirical paper.
Both address spatial data and mapping. UCR develops ArcGIS analysis and remote-sensing methods for environmental inquiry.
Both apply research to a local environment. UCR teams investigate a partner-supplied delta sustainability question, rather than the specified GPM living-environment project.

UCR offers substantive statistics, qualitative methods and applied projects, shown against their strongest counterparts. No remaining selected course establishes this separate GPM research-methodology foundation.
Local and geological fieldwork do not reproduce the required GPM project with research during a foreign excursion.

The selected team project is already aligned to local applied research. No scheduled course provides the individual 18-EC GPM thesis; optional independent research is shown separately under the standard comparison rule.
Global flows, political economy and European space
Both examine economic mechanisms relevant to globalisation and sustainability. UCR introduces markets and macroeconomics without the dedicated urban-economic framing.
Open-economy macroeconomics addresses an identifiable economic part of globalisation; UCR does not reproduce the integrated human-geographic study of globalising places.

European integration and its political institutions are a substantive part of both courses. UCR examines representation, legitimacy and EU policymaking rather than a specialist geography of borders and identities.
Introductory sociology includes migration among several topics, but does not establish a course centred on migration and social integration.
Public economics and open-economy macroeconomics do not establish sustained study of European cities, inter-city competition and urban economic geography.
Both address physical Earth processes relevant to environmental questions; UCR gives particular attention to geology and geological field observation.
Both examine how to intervene in sustainability problems. UCR develops governance diagnosis, stakeholder appraisal and policy advice, without reproducing the full GPM intervention-method sequence.
Selected courses provide social and environmental theories, but no sufficiently direct counterpart to this integrated spatial and environmental approaches course.
Social theory and empirical environmental analysis do not establish the component’s specific spatial and environmental theorising function.
Applied spatial engineering does not by itself establish the dedicated application of spatial theories in this theory-sequence culmination.
Genuine open elective space has no predetermined substantive counterpart.

notes.text: UCR combines relevant social sciences, environmental science, GIS, spatial engineering and delta research. Radboud GPM supplies a dedicated geographic and planning sequence, foreign fieldwork and an individual geography thesis. The alternatives offer related academic paths with important differences in specialist depth and research structure.

audience.programmeDescription: Geography, Planning and Environment examines how people shape places and how social, economic and environmental processes interact. This comparison follows the Globalisation route, alongside shared theory, methods, fieldwork and an independent thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: One UCR programme combines global social change, public decisions, GIS, spatial engineering and applied environmental research. The other concentrates on environmental science, water, energy and sustainability transitions. Both offer relevant academic study with different specialist priorities. They do not reproduce Radboud’s dedicated geographic theory, urban planning, specialist migration and border studies, required fieldwork abroad or 18-EC individual geography thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The selected route totals 180 EC: 60 EC in each year, including 30 EC of open study and an 18-EC thesis. Thesis entry requires the named academic-skills, methodology and statistics requirements and at least 120 programme EC. Fieldwork abroad is required; destinations vary. An internship and geography teacher training are optional choices, not compulsory parts of this pathway.
